content.Aktuell_miltenberg_title: Ursula Jüngst. In Search of the Horizon.
content.Aktuell_snippet91:
In 2026, Ursula Jüngst, who has already received multiple awards for her work, looks back on 40 years of intense striving for painterly expression. The museums in Miltenberg present not only previously unknown works from her current creative phase, but also trace her artistic path by placing newer works in dialogue with early paintings. These energetic works lead viewers into a fascinating state of self-forgetfulness. They celebrate painting, and again and again in the free, vibrant color forms and nuanced chromatic constellations there is the opportunity to discover a new "horizon". With her emotionally powerful paintings, the artist succeeds in setting hope and confidence against the terrors of world events. For the museums in Miltenberg, it is a great stroke of luck to be able to dedicate a major exhibition to this daughter of the town, especially in our difficult times.

A publication accompanying the exhibition is in preparation.

content.Aktuell_snippet64:
Insights into the exhibition "Malen gegen die Dunkelheit"

The exhibition presents around thirty paintings, some of them multipart, by the artist Ursula Jüngst, who lives and works in Nuremberg and Barcelona.
Within contemporary art, Ursula Jüngst's painting is distinctive for its luminosity and her striking brushstroke. Similar in length and width, the brushstroke is her artistic building block, enabling her to shape the subtlest emotions with great sensitivity and fullness. The emotional depth of her paintings is enriched by the flowing traces she employs.
She is able to transform traces that evoke blood and tears into lines of encounter and finally into something like fishing lines of light.
Her paintings, such as the cycle "Mariupol" or the works "Zeig mir deine Wunde" and "Dies irae, dies illa", reflect urgent existential questions of our society. In this exhibition, Ursula Jüngst's works enter into an exciting dialogue with the historical works from the museum collection and open up new ways of seeing.
Her paintings touch us deeply in our humanity.

Would you like to book a guided tour of the special exhibition?
Then please contact 05251 125-1400 or museum@erzbistum-paderborn.de

content.Aktuell_snippet51:
In her latest works, the Nuremberg painter Ursula Jüngst engages intensely with the crises of our immediate present: in the ten-part monumental painting "Schreck - Covid 19", for example, she experiments both with format and with the process of applying paint, which was carried out from a fixed distance using a telescopic pole. The struggle with the canvas, which metaphorically also stands for the tension of the coronavirus pandemic, unfolds as a forceful dramaturgy of color ranging from delicate to aggressive tones, executed in countless brush gestures that collide as compositional forms.
Here Ursula Jüngst is entirely in her element: generating opposing energies through arrangements of complex brushstrokes, impasto or glazed applications of color, and confidently guided flowing traces. Her painterly interventions do grant chance a role, but translate it into a consciously controlled pictorial structure and composition that remains classical in this sense and yet contemporary. With an introductory essay by the art historian Erich Schneider.

Edited by Erich Schneider. Published by modo Verlag.
200 pages, 136 illustrations, German / English
Portrait format 24 x 30 cm, hardcover, thread-sewn binding.

content.ArtKa_2017_snippet69:
Within contemporary art, Ursula Jüngst, who has been exploring painterly positions for more than thirty years, occupies a special place because of her distinctive visual language. Her paintings are powerful in their decisiveness. They show a creative handling of a broad spectrum of intense colors that follow inner impulses. Her knowledge of color relationships and their effect enriches them further.

The current trademark of the artist, who lives in Nuremberg and Barcelona, is her brushstrokes, similar in length and width. Through repetition and rhythm they acquire formal meaning. The brushwork takes on the status of a building block. It is her module, which can be combined in form and function. Art criticism highlights this innovative contribution and quite rightly speaks of the "brushstroke as a world formula".

With this broad brushstroke, Ursula Jüngst has taken an important step. Color and form are available as autonomous means. In contrast to a representation close to nature, they stand independently of time and place as living bodies of color and form. Articulated emotional values channel themselves into brush movements.
content.ArtKa_2017_snippet70:
In a kind of dance of color, the experimental painter surrenders to the process of encountering colors. She investigates the effect of different tonal nuances and is repeatedly surprised by her own discoveries.

Numerous strokes organize themselves, in changing directions and varying density of paint application, into a flowing together. Individual brush marks often contain traces of colors blending into one another. The color progression of single brushstrokes can change. They may approach the neighboring color, be related to it, or set themselves off in complementary contrast. In the variety thus gained and in the complexity of their relationships, they generate an increasingly shimmering effect.

The paintings break open what is familiar and invite free associations. They address fundamental states of human existence and are an expression of modern life. We become participants in a celebration of painting.

Bert Schlichtenmaier, Stuttgart

content.Begegnungsspuren_snippet31:
Painting is for me a way of reflecting on the world. To discover and experience new things, to remember and clarify. To try to get to the bottom of being. The picture develops in the dialogue between the colors, the support and myself.
Because of the experience of the corona lockdown and the consequences associated with it - for example, that it was forbidden even to visit seriously ill relatives - my democratic basic feeling was shaken. My brushstroke, my artistic formula for the world, began to slip. The basic module of my compositions started to wobble.
In places, my brush marks now begin to flow. Fine, careful, trembling traces of flow bring something nervous and fragile into the pictorial structure and make the distinct brushstrokes vibrate. Traces of encounter. Purposeful, self-confident rivulets become strings of sound, fishing lines of light, and lassos for my brush chords. Attempts at new forms of encounter.
content.Corona_snippet15:
Schreck - Covid 19. Everything changed. Within Europe the borders closed. Schengen no longer counted. Shutdown. Locking away. Alone. Daily images of death in the media. Turning away instead of turning toward one another. Bergamo. Madrid. Hotspot after hotspot. Isolation became normal. Distance became charity. A society of distance.
My brushes are extended to two meters. A red line marks the distance of two meters from the painting surface. 10 panels. 10 like two families together. 10 like a meeting group. Each panel is proportionally similar to a human being. To a coffin. The individual panels are separated and yet belong together. The shock is deep and struggles with the light. The stillness is threatening. I paint with the distance brush. It is difficult to cope with distance. The application of paint becomes rougher. Immersed in painting, I sometimes step across the distancing line. That allows me to conjure the delicate fusion of colors. Keeping one's distance is hard.

content.Literatur_tableGrid91snippet1:
Großes Orchester

For a painter living in the Renaissance or the Baroque period, staging great themes on great surfaces belonged to the challenges he regularly had to face - or perhaps was even allowed to face. One need only think of Michelangelo's works in the Sistine Chapel in Rome or, to bridge to the end of that epoch, Tiepolo's fresco in the staircase of the Würzburg Residence. Timeless fame was achieved above all by an artist who excelled in this field as well.
With the end of the Baroque period, the great ceiling fresco also disappeared; other tasks moved to the foreground for art. After art had once again detached itself from decoration in Classicism and Historicism - and leaving aside entirely what Nazi monumentalism produced - free art in the second half of the twentieth century again sought the large format: Georg Meistermann led the way between 1953 and 1956 with his immense stained-glass window "Pfingsten" in St. Kilian in Schweinfurt. From the 1970s onward Hans Hartung created his huge abstract-expressionist works in Antibes, and between 1989 and 1991 Fred Thieler painted "Nachthimmel" in the Munich Residence.
And then there is an artist like Ursula Jüngst, who since studying with Hans Peter Reuter at the Nuremberg Academy has, out of inner conviction and simply because she wants to, repeatedly placed large formats at the center of her work. An early example of her independent artistic practice is the work "Vulkangeflüster" from 2003, which developed into a panoramic painting fifteen meters long and two meters high. This work already appears unusually mature and anticipates much of what continues to characterize Ursula Jüngst's oeuvre in a consistent further development to this day.
Her paintings come into being over a long period of time. She stretches the canvases herself and applies several layers of primer in order to give the support its own breath from the very beginning. Then, in the actual painterly process, she acts in an interplay between open experiment and consciously controlled brush marks. If, in this dialogue, her eye remains stuck on a single brushstroke, then the picture is not yet finished. In her view, it is only successful once the gaze can move through the picture with ease.

content.Literatur_tableGrid83snippet1:
Licht ist dein Kleid

Light is the garment you wear. You spread out the heavens like a tent; you build your chambers above the waters. You ride on the clouds as on a chariot and come forth on the wings of the wind, you make winds your messengers and flames of fire your servants; you founded the earth upon its firm ground so that it shall not totter forever and ever.
content.Literatur_tableGrid30snippet1:
Ursula Jüngst, who works in Nuremberg and Barcelona, has made an innovative contribution to the formative power of color. For more than thirty years, the artist, born in Miltenberg in 1965, has explored painterly positions. Her paintings are expressions of the modern attitude to life in the present. They address fundamental questions and can be understood as "Elementare Akkorde".
Her pictures are recognizable by their brushstroke. Over the past ten years it has become a trademark. In a kind of dance of color, the experimental painter enters into the process of encountering colors, which for her are carriers of sensation. They appear shimmering, provocative or tender. They mix and organize themselves into a flowing together and radiate an enlivening effect.
In 2013 Ursula Jüngst resumed her engagement with large format. A characteristic feature is being "in the middle of the picture", being swept along and experiencing the orchestra of colors intensely, sensually tangible and plastically relief-like in the room.
The publication not only presents new works by the artist, it also shows where they were created and, in detail, how the different colors react to one another. Between the works, essays and interviews through which one can approach the artist's oeuvre, there are also the painter's own comments on her pictures: "The cicada sings its midday song. Shrill. Cobalt blue bites red. The sun is glaring and hot. Time seems to have stopped, the moment endless."
content.Literatur_tableGrid38snippet1:
Farbe meine Sprache - Unendliche Impressionen

"Colour as the object of painting is the constituent subject in the works of Ursula Jüngst. Her latest works originated in this context: a multitude of strong, nearly equally long, straight brushstrokes placed next to or above each other in a controlled way - a meticulous technique that she elaborated during the last two years. With intensive colours, rich in contrast, she models complex colour fields and structures that look freer and more concrete in her current phase of work. The colours blend in a subtle way, because traces of the already painted colours flash up again and again from underneath the lower layers. With a comprehensive system of singular brushstrokes, huge abstract colour landscapes rich in contrast come into being. They align with traces of movement and make the process of painting visible. The maximal size of these pictures is guided by the radius of gestural movement while painting. Coloured areas form the basic composition, which is then structured by the accumulation of individual brushstrokes. With impressionistic gesture Ursula Jüngst adds stroke to stroke, colour to colour, and models iridescent colour fields with thick applications of paint repeated hundreds and thousands of times. She develops these fields harmoniously within a range from yellow to red, from green to blue, or contrasts autonomous structures with complementary effects, light-dark or cold-warm contrasts and independent colour values..."

Christoph Schneider, Freiburg, August 2011
content.Literatur_tableGrid45snippet1:
Sternengeburt

"Looking at the new paintings by Ursula Jüngst from the years 2007 and 2008, one experiences a true flush of colors. Color is and remains the painter's source of impulse. Even more clearly than in her earlier oeuvre, the latest works reveal an intensification of chromatic energy.
Alongside this richness of colors, the painter's brushwork is a decisive, tone-setting instrument. Compared with works from previous years, the ductus has shortened, appears more concise and heightens the energetic coloring through its swirling traces of movement. The brushstroke is immediate: it dynamizes the picture surface, it orders, just as it simultaneously questions any system..."

Barbara Leicht M.A., curator, Kunstmuseum Erlangen
content.Literatur_tableGrid75snippet1:
Die Azulen

...In the second large group of works, the "Azulen", to which this catalogue is devoted, the artist consciously tries to keep such associations largely at bay. At first glance they appear much calmer because of their relatively monochrome color fields, created through several, yet much thinner layers of paint.
Closer observation, however, teaches otherwise, because the large color fields that appear monochrome reveal within a single hue a rich play of nuances and again and again allow the layers of color underneath to resonate through them, so that the viewer's eye wanders on a true journey of discovery through luminous spaces of color...

Dr. Cornelia Vagt-Beck,
art historian
content.Literatur_tableGrid79snippet1:
Zeichnungen

...My drawings emerge parallel to my large oil paintings. They are really like a "diary". In drawing, I try to respond spontaneously to impressions, to make feelings and thoughts visible that are still veiled even to myself, and to understand them myself...

Ursula Jüngst
content.Literatur_tableGrid103snippet1:
Archäologie des Unbewußten

...Courage in the face of the risk of failure characterizes Ursula Jüngst's work. She exposes herself to color, lives within it. The pictures develop without a fixed concept, purely from the act of painting and from constant dialogue with colors. In this process, enigmatic forms are born from superimposed colors and the ductus of the brush - forms that seem tangible and yet elude clear definition, comparable to cloud images. Evidently, a force emanates from these pictures, rooted in the intensity and range of their colors, from Mediterranean brightness to the darkest tunnel of death. Many viewers seem to gain an intimation, in the aesthetics of Ursula Jüngst's pictures, of the "archaeology of the unconscious" in its depth-psychological, metaphysical and religious dimension. Encountering these pictures opens existential spaces within us through aesthetic experience. In this respect, Ursula Jüngst's works differ refreshingly from contemporary currents of post-structural arbitrariness. They show that the possibilities of color and painting - currently often pushed aside in the art world in favor of ready-mades, concept art, computer animation and the like - are far from exhausted and in fact allow for new departures. They are modern because they address human beings in their emptiness and metaphysical homelessness.

Dr. Karl v. Schmölling

content.Statement_snippet35:
While painting, I pull the ground out from under myself, making upside-down placements and complementary collisions. In doing so, I lose what I had already found. How do I deal with decay and destruction? What happens when my previous experiences and orientations no longer hold true? It presses in on me from all sides. I let streams of color flow and am compelled to redefine the compositional structure. I explore the unknown.

Ursula Jüngst, March 2026
content.Statement_snippet28:
Our world seems to be undergoing a reordering, and I, too, redefine points of orientation in my works. During the painting process I repeatedly determine what is above and below all over again - especially when I feel that a flowing trace should move against gravity. While painting I scrape along the edge of chaos and search for new bearings. In doing so, my brush marks and flowing traces shape the rhythmic structure of my paintings. Above and below, front and back begin to vibrate together. In the interplay of paint traces and colors, I try to find the horizon.

Ursula Jüngst, February 2025
content.Statement_snippet30:
With brush and colors, placements and flowing traces, I venture into places and feelings unfamiliar to me. In doing so, I experience terror, transience, pain and fear, but also joy, tenderness and strength. I am touched and able to touch, to take part, to respect, to discover, to resist. It is my way of encountering the world with questions and also with love.
I want to paint against the dark, the tornness, the speechlessness, the annihilating cold. Painting carries within it the power of renewal. I see my brush marks and flowing lines as forms through which to explore new possibilities of encounter.


Ursula Jüngst, March 2024
content.Statement_snippet31: Scar, 2024, Oil on canvas, 120 x 90 cm
content.Statement_snippet23: Painting at the nerve of the times
content.Statement_snippet21:
My paintings - even if they may at first glance look like plays of color - are my commentary on the current crisis-ridden state of our world. They are painterly interventions into the events of my present.

I am not a storyteller and I do not take the detour of representational depiction. In the act of painting I trust the forces inherent in the material and intensify them.

For me, painting is a field of experimentation for questions of being. In a balancing act between control and loss of control, between preserving, discovering, shaping and destroying, I conduct my artistic means. These are my distinctive brushstrokes and my dancing traces of flow, which are reworked several times in the painterly process and thus intensify the expression. One might see the brushstrokes as stand-ins for people with all their different experiences and possibilities. The flowing lines create new forms of encounter, making the subtlest stirrings and also inevitability visible. My artistic means of expression are consciously shaped right to the outermost edges of the format and carry respect and consideration.

Together with the brush marks and traces of flow, the deliberately chosen colors become mediators of rich and subtle sensations and developed attitudes. In the mutual permeation of colors and forms, a luminous, energetic tonal space of color opens up. Free of spatial localization, this compositional structure oscillates and thus creates ever new possibilities of viewing. At the same time light plays in the image, changing from front to back, penetrating the pictorial space and spreading outward.

In my paintings I try to find an adequate expression for these burdensome times and to paint against dark experiences - setting the hopeful force of light and of uplifting wonder against powerlessness, decay and aggression.

Ursula Jüngst, July 2023
content.Statement_snippet15:
I want my painting to reach people and meet them where their feelings are today.
Painting is a language that speaks directly to people's hearts. Art is a way of keeping doors open, even where communication no longer works. For me, painting is also an expression of love and of the conviction that art contains the power to counter absurdity and arbitrariness.
content.Statement_snippet17: The painting "Schlaf mein Kind auch wenn der Teufel lacht" (already painted in 2020) fits our times exactly. In this painting I try to express the feelings of a mother - of a protector - who attempts to safeguard her child, the dearest and most vulnerable thing, in spite of all adversity, all madness, all fears and all impossibility.
content.Statement_snippet20:
"For heaven's sake" - "Um Himmels willen" - an exclamation that may once have seemed emptied out, but which in the face of one's own powerlessness and loss of composure gains new meaning precisely now. In this painting, created at the end of last year, vehement dark brushstrokes are set down and in places begin to flow, evoking tears and the passage of time, perhaps also its decay. Yet the frightening black is confronted by fresh life-affirming yellow, delicate pink and green, the color of incipient love. The flowing traces are transformed and become fishing lines of light.

Ursula Jüngst, August 2022
